final_candidates.decision_summary: K119 is the catalytic PLP-binding lysine. Replacing it with alanine should directly abolish catalysis without intentionally disrupting global folding.
Y223 is positioned in the catalytic core. Alanine removes its aromatic and hydrogen-bonding functionality and is expected to severely impair active-site chemistry.
Replacing the catalytic K119 with glutamate eliminates its PLP-binding amine and reverses the local charge. This should abolish activity, although it may perturb the active site more than K119A.

stop_reason.detail: Further LLM-only iteration is unlikely to improve the mechanistically strong Top-3.

history.rationale: K119 is the catalytic lysine that forms the internal aldimine with PLP. Removing its reactive side chain should directly abolish catalysis while minimizing gross structural disruption.
K119 is the catalytic PLP-binding lysine, so alanine substitution should directly eliminate catalysis while avoiding deliberate global unfolding.
Replacing the catalytic lysine with a negatively charged residue prevents normal PLP Schiff-base chemistry and is likely to create an unfavorable active-site environment.
Charge reversal at the catalytic PLP-binding lysine should abolish activity, although it may perturb the active-site structure more than K119A.
R266 is an active-site residue important for substrate/cofactor organization and catalytic communication. Charge reversal should strongly disrupt productive catalysis.
R266E is a strong charge-reversal perturbation in the catalytic domain, but complete abolition is less certain than for direct catalytic-site substitutions.
Y223 contributes to the PLP-centered active-site environment. Removing its aromatic and hydroxyl groups should impair cofactor positioning and catalytic chemistry.
Y223 lies in the catalytic core and alanine removes its aromatic and hydrogen-bonding functionality, making it a strong mechanistically targeted loss-of-function candidate.
T257 lies in the conserved PLP-active-site region. Proline substitution should disrupt both local backbone geometry and catalytic hydrogen-bonding interactions.
Proline in the conserved catalytic-core segment could strongly impair local geometry, but it carries greater risk of destabilizing the protein.
T260 is another conserved residue adjacent to the PLP catalytic center. Introducing proline is expected to distort the active-site loop and eliminate its polar side-chain contribution.
T260P may disrupt the glycine-rich catalytic-core region, though its effect on activity versus overall folding remains uncertain.

G307 is in the catalytic core and requires conformational flexibility, as indicated by the severe effects associated with substitutions at this site. Proline should impose a particularly damaging backbone constraint.
G307P is likely structurally disruptive in the catalytic domain, making it less attractive when preservation of a viable folded protein is desired.

C52 is a heme axial ligand in human CBS. Removing its sulfur ligand should disrupt heme incorporation and allosteric integrity, strongly reducing activity although the catalytic domain may retain some residual function.
H65 provides the second axial ligand to the regulatory heme. Alanine substitution should compromise heme binding and native enzyme organization.
D376 is located in the catalytic core and is associated with severe functional sensitivity. Proline should combine loss of the acidic side chain with local structural distortion.
D376P lacks a comparably direct catalytic rationale and may primarily compromise structural integrity.
